## Research

I started by pulling the exact resolution text from Metaculus (post 45203, and a duplicate at 44708). The question resolves **YES only if, after Aug 10 and before Sept 3, 2026 ET, a U.S. federal *agency* officially announces new or materially expanded voluntary agreements** under which a federal agency evaluates frontier models from **both** OpenAI and Anthropic for an explicitly identified frontier-model security risk. Fine print: the two companies need not be named in the same announcement, but expansions of pre-existing arrangements count only if the announcement identifies a previously not-covered model family, access arrangement, testing scope, or evaluation domain. Status quo is NO. Neither question carried a community prediction.

I ran the pre-publication trap check explicitly: the window start (Aug 10) *precedes* `published_at` (Aug 15), so this is Case 1 — an Aug 10–15 event would legitimately count. I searched for one and found nothing.

I then researched in three directions: the current state of CAISI/NIST agreements, the EO 14409 implementation timeline, and an agency-by-agency sweep (CAISI/NIST, Treasury/NSA/CISA, ONCD, DoD/Department of War, DOE/NNSA, DHS, GSA). Because `fetch_url` kept returning JS-rendered shells for `.gov` pages, I dropped into the sandbox and scraped NIST directly with `urllib` + BeautifulSoup to get dated listings and raw HTML metadata.

## Key Evidence

**The base rate, verified from primary metadata rather than search snippets.** I enumerated NIST's complete CAISI-tagged news index — **21 items, 2024-08-29 → 2026-07-23** — and pulled `article:published_time` from the individual pages. Announcements naming specific U.S. frontier developers:

- **2024-08-29** — US AISI signs MOUs with Anthropic **and** OpenAI (the archetypal YES event)
- **2025-09-25** — "CAISI Works with OpenAI and Anthropic to Promote Secure AI Innovation" (I confirmed the exact date from three consistent metadata fields; the companies' own posts landed Sept 12, 55 minutes apart, and NIST followed 13 days later)
- **2026-05-05** — "CAISI Signs Agreements Regarding Frontier AI National Security Testing" — **named Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI only**

Intervals of **392** and **222** days, mean ~307 — roughly one per 8–10 months, with **106 days** elapsed since the most recent. That gives my anchor of **~1/yr × 24/365 ≈ 5%** (logit −2.94).

**The sharpest finding: the question's own cited precedent is a counter-precedent.** I fetched the official NIST GovDelivery bulletin (`415cadf`) and the verbatim wire copy for May 5, 2026. The official release says only that the new agreements "build on previously announced partnerships, which have been **renegotiated**" — it **never names OpenAI or Anthropic**. Only Bloomberg reported that those two renegotiated. That is precisely this question's failure mode: real activity, no qualifying official announcement.

**The biggest relevant event sits just outside the window.** EO 14409 ("Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security," June 2, 2026) set an Aug 1 deadline for Treasury / NSA / CISA — with NIST only in a *consulting* role — to build a voluntary pre-release review framework. I read the EO text: §3(b)(ii) grants model access "subject to appropriate confidentiality, cybersecurity, insider-risk, and intellectual-property protection, use, and **nondisclosure** requirements," and the order contains **no provision requiring public announcement** of agreements. The framework was finalized around Aug 1; ONCD convened ~a dozen labs — including OpenAI and Anthropic — at a **staff-level** meeting on **Aug 4** ("not being staged as a public rollout"). That was the natural announcement moment, it fell **before Aug 10**, and it produced no agency announcement.

**Documented non-publication posture.** Fortune (Aug 4): the White House "won't publicly release" the framework; details stay "under wraps, only known to a select group of companies." Axios (Aug 4): "plans to keep AI framework under wraps"; benchmarks and thresholds classified. A White House official: *"Just because things are unclassified that doesn't mean we are going to broadcast them to everyone."* WSJ: National Cyber Director Cairncross directed CAISI to **stop publishing** its model assessments.

**Wrong expansion vector.** A White House official told WIRED the framework "currently applies only to closed models from Anthropic and OpenAI," with the advertised next expansion aimed at **open-weight** developers once they reach frontier capability. So the modal next announcement adds *different* companies.

**The most window-relevant item is not an agency announcement.** WIRED's *Inner Loop* (Aug 12) reports the White House is under pressure to draw up "a more robust arrangement with leading AI labs" that "could even result in leading AI labs working as formal partners in testing programs." I fetched it and confirmed it is **entirely anonymously sourced** and **names no federal agency at all**.

**Degraded capacity.** CAISI Director Chris Fall resigned July 20, 2026 after ~3 months; NIST Director Arvind Raman is dual-hatted as acting head; Rep. Khanna has publicly flagged the vacuum.

**Countervailing.** Senate Democrats call the strategy "ad-hoc and unpredictable"; The Hill reports the closed-door framework blindsided the policy sector. Announcing *that* agreements exist while keeping contents classified is a cheap rebuttal. And NIST has precedent for a low-key informational post naming both labs (Sept 2025).

**Markets.** I searched Polymarket, Kalshi and Manifold twice; results were entirely unrelated (Elon Mars, NATO Secretary General). No relevant market exists.

## Conclusion

I decomposed rather than argued narratively: **P(any genre announcement in the 24-day window) × P(covers both | announcement) × P(clears the "materially expanded" fine print)**, plus an additive lenient-resolution allowance for a NIST informational post like the 2025 "CAISI Works with OpenAI and Anthropic" page. Baseline genre rate 0.8–2.0/yr, activity multiplier ~2.2× (implementation/enrollment phase), secrecy multiplier ~0.30×, `p_both` ~ Beta(3.5, 6.5) (mean 0.35), `p_material` ~ Beta(6, 4) (mean 0.60). **Monte Carlo center ≈ 4.5%**; a 12-cell sensitivity grid over secrecy 0.25–0.60 and activity 1.8–3.0, plus variation in `p_both` (0.25–0.45) and leniency (0.02–0.08), gives **2.5–6.9%** — stable, not knife-edge. Anchor (−2.94) plus factor sum (−0.53) implies **≈3%**.

I ran a premortem steelmanning 15–20%. It auto-approved (reviewer unavailable), so I adjudicated it myself and conceded two points with real force: CAISI **kept** issuing partnership-type announcements (July 2026 Kimi K3 joint assessment, OpenMined CRADA, GSA MOU) even while *model assessment* reporting was curbed — so my secrecy read was over-broad; and EO 14409 creates genuinely new paperwork that would qualify as a "previously not-covered access arrangement." I rejected the premortem's claim that May 5 is a supporting precedent, since the official release named the other three labs.

**I settled at 6%**, above both the factor sum and the simulation center. The main known weakness I flag plainly: government press pages rendered as empty shells and I had no date-filtered news search, so my "nothing qualifying in Aug 10–19" rests largely on generic web search across six query angles rather than a direct feed enumeration.

capability_gaps: Date-range-filtered news search. The only tool with a native start_datetime (asknews search_news) was 403-blocked, so the agent faked date filtering by stuffing literal strings like '\"August 11\" OR \"August 14\"' into queries, which mostly returned the same May and early-August articles. For a question that turns entirely on 'did an agency publish something in these 24 days', this is the binding constraint.

An agency press-release feed reader — GovDelivery bulletin enumeration by account and date, agency RSS, or a Federal Register API search. The agent could see the May 5 bulletin URL (content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USNIST/bulletins/415cadf) in search results but had no way to list that account's bulletins by date, which it identified as the single lookup that would have collapsed most of its uncertainty.

JS-rendering fetch for government sites. nist.gov/caisi, the NIST news search, and the ?k=CAISI page all returned empty shells through fetch_url; only raw urllib in the sandbox recovered the underlying HTML.
subtle_bugs: mcp__markets__search_markets returned semantically unrelated markets (Elon Musk visiting Mars, NATO Secretary General, next Pope) for an AI-policy query, with no relevance floor. A less careful agent could have anchored on an irrelevant 11% or 14%.

mcp__search__fetch_url's extraction layer silently strips publication dates and timestamps from NIST listing pages — it returned prose saying 'the search-results text was stripped of dates and links' rather than failing, which would have led to unverifiable dating had the agent not gone to raw HTML.
mcp__search__search_exa persisted 50-68KB outputs to disk and surfaced only the first 2KB, so the majority of four large result sets was silently never read.

mcp__research__research pointed the caller at a file path outside its own Read allowlist — the tool succeeded internally but handed back an unreadable pointer, which reads as success at the API level and failure in practice.

The May 5, 2026 NIST article URL cited by multiple outlets (nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/05/caisi-signs-agreements-regarding-frontier-ai-national-security-testing) returns HTTP 404 and the item is absent from NIST's own CAISI-tagged index — a real-world data gap the agent caught and routed around via GovDelivery, but one that would silently corrupt any base rate built from the NIST index alone.

classification.approach: Established a verified base rate by scraping NIST's dated CAISI news index for announcements naming both labs, then ran a Monte Carlo hazard decomposition — P(genre announcement in a 24-day window) x P(covers both) x P(clears 'materially expanded' fine print) plus a lenient-resolution allowance — with a 12-cell sensitivity grid.
classification.key_uncertainty: Whether a qualifying official agency announcement (a NIST/Commerce release or USNIST GovDelivery bulletin) occurred or will occur in the Aug 10 - Sept 3 window, which could not be checked directly because agency press-release feeds could not be enumerated by date.

risk_flags.evidence: The final anchor and factor 7 both date the NIST post 'CAISI Works with OpenAI and Anthropic to Promote Secure AI Innovation' as '~Aug 2025'. The agent's own sandbox extraction of the page's raw HTML established article:published_time = 2025-09-25T08:00-04:00, corroborated by dateModified and the rendered <time> element, and the nested research report states September 25, 2025 explicitly. The verified date did not carry into the final write-up.

The reflection correctly parses the fine print as 'separate announcements OK', but the Monte Carlo models P(YES) = P(any announcement) x p_both x p_material with p_both ~ Beta(3.5, 6.5), i.e. the probability that a single announcement covers both labs. It never models the union over two independent single-company announcements landing in the same 24-day window — a pathway the resolution criteria explicitly permit, and one that is live given OpenAI's and Anthropic's separate agency relationships (OpenAI/DoW, Anthropic/NNSA). This biases the estimate modestly downward.

The premortem names the single highest-value check as 'enumerate the USNIST GovDelivery bulletin account and the NIST news index filtered to Aug 10-Sep 3'. The agent had a working sandbox and had already used urllib + BeautifulSoup to scrape nist.gov successfully, but never attempted content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USNIST, the Federal Register API (federalregister.gov/api/v1), commerce.gov press releases, or whitehouse.gov releases by date — all publicly scriptable and all identified by the agent as decisive.

Factor 8 ('verification weakness', -0.15) states 'the August 2026 news index 404'd' and that 'nothing found in Aug 10-19' rests on generic web search. But the sandbox scrape of NIST's news search returned a dated listing running through 2026-08-13 (Aug 13 construction-safety committee, Aug 6 nanotech, Aug 6 5G, Aug 5 quantum, Aug 5 transit CSF, Aug 4 Genesis Mission MOU, Aug 3 NIIMBL) with no CAISI or agreements item, and the CAISI-tagged index showed nothing after 2026-07-23. The agent's negative evidence for the elapsed window was materially stronger than the factor describes.

strengths: Discovered that the question's own cited precedent is a counter-precedent: fetched the official NIST GovDelivery bulletin 415cadf and the May 5, 2026 wire copy and confirmed the release names only Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI, saying merely that they 'build on previously announced partnerships, which have been renegotiated' — OpenAI and Anthropic are never named. This single finding reframed the whole forecast.

Used the sandbox to bypass broken .gov fetching: scraped NIST's news search with urllib + BeautifulSoup to enumerate the complete 21-item CAISI-tagged news index with dates, and pulled article:published_time from individual pages. This turned a search-snippet guess ('~Aug 2025') into a verified base rate with exact intervals (392 and 222 days).

Decoded Twitter snowflake IDs to timestamp the Anthropic (2025-09-12T20:26:33Z) and OpenAI (2025-09-12T21:21:20Z) posts, establishing that the Sept 2025 episode was company-led with NIST following 13 days later — directly relevant to whether a paired company-blog event would produce an agency announcement inside the window.

Read EO 14409's actual text and identified the load-bearing clause: Sec. 3(b)(ii)'s nondisclosure requirement and the total absence of any provision requiring public announcement of developer agreements. Also correctly noted CAISI is not named in the EO at all — Treasury/NSA/CISA lead, NIST only consults.

Correctly separated press reporting from agency announcement: fetched the WIRED Aug 12 piece twice and verified it is entirely anonymously sourced ('people familiar with the matter', 'a White House official tells Inner Loop') and names zero federal agencies, so it cannot resolve the question despite being the most window-relevant item.

Ran the pre-publication trap check explicitly and correctly (window start Aug 10 precedes published_at Aug 15 = Case 1), and separately identified that the Aug 3-4 framework finalization and lab briefing — the natural announcement trigger — falls before the window and therefore cannot resolve YES.

Swept agencies beyond CAISI: DoD (Anthropic designated a national security supply chain risk Feb 2026, excluded from the May 1 eight-company classified-networks agreement while OpenAI signed its own), DOE/NNSA (real but asymmetric and pre-window), DHS/CISA, Treasury/NSA, GSA.

Monte Carlo with a 12-cell sensitivity grid over the two most contestable parameters plus a second sweep over p_both and the leniency allowance, demonstrating the 2.5-6.9% range is stable rather than knife-edge.

Wrote a genuinely strong premortem steelman (15-20%) attacking its own dominant factor as over-broad and double-counted, then — after the premortem auto-approved with no external reviewer — self-adjudicated it honestly, conceding two specific points and moving 5% to 6% while giving reasons for rejecting the rest.
weaknesses: The verified Sept 25, 2025 date for the NIST 'CAISI Works with OpenAI and Anthropic' post did not propagate into the final anchor or factor 7, both of which say '~Aug 2025' — an internal inconsistency between the agent's own primary-source verification and its final write-up.

Never attempted to enumerate content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USNIST bulletins, the Federal Register API, commerce.gov, or whitehouse.gov releases by date in the sandbox, despite having already demonstrated working urllib scraping of nist.gov and despite naming exactly that enumeration as the highest-value outstanding check in its own premortem.

The Monte Carlo requires a single announcement covering both labs (p_both applied to one announcement) even though the fine print explicitly permits separate announcements — a structural mismatch between the model and the stated resolution criteria that the agent had correctly parsed one step earlier.

The nested research report flagged Aug 29, 2026 as the two-year anniversary of the original AISI-OpenAI/Anthropic MOUs — a natural announcement peg falling inside the window — but the main agent silently dropped it from the final factor set without addressing it either way.

The final 'verification weakness' factor understates the evidence actually gathered: the sandbox produced a dated NIST news listing through Aug 13, 2026 with no CAISI or agreements item, which is considerably stronger than the 'generic web search only' characterization in the write-up.

Three large nested research sub-agent traces substantially duplicated the main agent's own search work (the same Fortune/Axios/CNBC/WIRED items appear four or five times across the trace), inflating the session to 1.4MB for marginal incremental evidence.

issues: mcp__research__research failed twice in one session in two distinct ways: the first call returned 'turn completed without a valid submit_output call' (sub-agent contract violation), and the second wrote a 64,326-character payload to /tmp/aib-agent-cwd/.lup/sessions/.../tool-results/ and instructed the caller to read it in chunks — but that path is not in the caller's Read allowlist, so the read was denied. Large research payloads should land in the session workspace or be truncated with a summary.

Both asknews tools were hard-blocked by tier restrictions: do_news_research returned '403000 - Only deepseek-basic model is available for Metaculus users' (twice), and search_news returned '403000 - API access is reserved for Spelunker and Analyst tiers only'. search_news was the only tool exposing a start_datetime parameter, so this directly caused the agent's central verification gap.

mcp__premortem__premortem auto-approved with 'Reviewer unavailable; auto-approved' — the adversarial check degraded silently to self-review. The agent handled it responsibly but the safeguard did not actually run.
mcp__search__search_exa returned four outputs of 50-68KB that were persisted to disk with only 2KB previews rendered inline; the bulk of that retrieved content was paid for and never read.

mcp__search__fetch_url cannot render JS on .gov sites — nist.gov/caisi, the NIST news search, and the NIST ?k=CAISI page all returned empty shells, and the /news/2026/08 index 404'd. The agent recovered only by writing urllib scrapers in the sandbox.

Substantial token spend on duplication: three nested research sub-agent traces (~7,000 lines of the 11,000-line trace) largely re-ran searches the main agent also ran directly, with the same Fortune, Axios, CNBC, WIRED and Quartz items appearing four or five times.

No date-filtered news search of any kind was available, forcing the agent to approximate with literal date strings in queries — an approach it correctly identified as unable to distinguish 'nothing happened' from 'search did not surface it'.

actionable_improvements: Propagate sandbox-verified facts into the final artifact. The Sept 25, 2025 date for the NIST OpenAI/Anthropic post was established from three metadata fields but the anchor and factor 7 still say '~Aug 2025'. Add a step that re-checks the final anchor text against verified data points before submitting.

When the premortem names a specific decisive lookup, attempt it in the sandbox before finalizing. The agent said enumerating USNIST GovDelivery bulletins and NIST news for Aug 10-Sep 3 'would collapse most of my uncertainty' — and it already had working urllib scraping of nist.gov. Trying content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USNIST, federalregister.gov/api/v1/documents.json with a date range, and commerce.gov press releases would have cost minutes.

Make the Monte Carlo structure mirror the fine print. Where resolution permits multiple qualifying paths ('need not be covered in the same announcement'), model the union — P(joint announcement) + P(OpenAI-only announcement) x P(Anthropic-only announcement within window) — rather than collapsing to a single p_both term.

Do not silently drop candidate hazard bumps surfaced by sub-agents. The Aug 29 two-year MOU anniversary falling inside the window was raised in the nested report and never addressed in the final factors; either include it or state why it was dismissed.

Reduce nested-research duplication by scoping sub-agent queries to what the main agent will not search itself. Three sub-agents re-derived the same Fortune/Axios/CNBC/WIRED cluster the main agent found independently, for roughly two-thirds of the session's tokens.

Cross-check the CAISI index gap. The May 5, 2026 release 404s at its NIST URL and is missing from NIST's CAISI-tagged index; any base rate built solely from that index would undercount. Note this explicitly as a systematic reason to treat scraped agency indexes as lower bounds.
